segments.title: HMS Dreadnought's 12-inch starting point
segments.summary: HMS Dreadnought's 12-inch bore is compared with a head roughly 10 inches from top to chin.
segments.body: A head roughly 10 inches from top to chin supplies the opening scale reference. HMS Dreadnought's 12-inch gun then gives the first naval calibre, with a bore one foot across. The comparison establishes the scale for the larger gun diameters that follow.

evidence.note: The transcript introduces dreadnought gun calibres and identifies Dreadnought's 12-inch gun as the first comparison.

segments.title: Orion's 13.5-inch guns and the half-inch step to 14 inches
segments.summary: The Orion class's 13.5-inch calibre is close to 14 inches, although the half-inch difference is described as enough to matter.
segments.body: The Orion class supplies the 13.5-inch example after Dreadnought's 12-inch starting point. A 14-inch bore looks only slightly larger in the comparison. The extra half-inch is nevertheless described as enough to matter, without quantifying its effect on gunnery performance.

evidence.note: The transcript compares Orion's 13.5-inch gun with a 14-inch gun and says the difference still matters.

segments.title: The Queen Elizabeth class's 15-inch shell width
segments.summary: The Queen Elizabeth class's 15-inch shells are illustrated as almost the width of a chest.
segments.body: The Queen Elizabeth class supplies the 15-inch example, with a shell width described as almost the distance across a chest. This is the next increase after the Orion and 14-inch comparisons. The joke about how much a hit would hurt then leads into the larger 16-inch example.

evidence.note: The transcript identifies the Queen Elizabeth class's 15-inch guns and compares the shell width with a chest.

segments.title: Colorado's 16-inch gun in human scale
segments.summary: The Colorado class's 16-inch bore prompts a joke that two heads might fit inside it.
segments.body: The Colorado class supplies the 16-inch example, an inch wider than the Queen Elizabeth class's gun. The diameter prompts the suggestion that two heads might fit inside the bore. The two-head remark is a tentative joke about scale, continuing the informal comparison with a person's head before the move to 18 inches.

evidence.note: The transcript identifies the Colorados' 16-inch guns and uses a two-head comparison for their diameter.

segments.title: HMS Furious and Yamato in the 18-inch comparison
segments.summary: The final comparison groups HMS Furious and Yamato under 18 inches and illustrates that width as roughly shoulder to shoulder.
segments.body: HMS Furious and Yamato close the guide in its 18-inch grouping. The illustrated diameter is roughly the distance from shoulder to shoulder, completing the increase from Dreadnought's 12-inch starting point. The final joke again connects the projectile's width with the prospect of being hit by it.

evidence.note: The transcript names HMS Furious and Yamato as examples with 18-inch guns and compares the diameter with shoulder width.
